page_placements.theme: Safety, robustness, calibration and behavioral stability require separate scaling accounts

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own downstream-task results as language-model size increases, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss or reproduce the original scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses and cites prior scaling-law results, including Figure 1 adapted from Kaplan et al.; cited arithmetic, MMLU, program-synthesis, modality, and transfer results are not its own and are excluded. Its own recommendation and recidivism experiments report task-performance outcomes by scale. Toxicity and fairness-ratio results are recorded as findings about scaling, but do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: Its own experiments, zero-shot MovieLens recommendation and few-shot COMPAS recidivism prediction, report downstream task performance across Anthropic LM sizes. That bears on V6 in task settings not used by the originals. The loss-scaling material (Fig. 1, adapted from Kaplan) and the abrupt-capability examples (Fig. 2) are cited, not the study's own results. T3 rather than T2: the tasks are new settings, not a different method for the original loss question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors argue that loss on a broad distribution scales predictably and correlates loosely with average task performance, while specific capabilities can emerge abruptly and inputs and outputs are open-ended. Harmful properties (bias, toxicity) can scale alongside useful capabilities. Their own experiments illustrate smooth task gains (recommendation, recidivism) and rising bias and toxicity with scale.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce the original pretraining-loss scaling method; it reports downstream task performance across model sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: The recidivism experiment compares prompts that include versus exclude race; the authors report no significant difference in predictive accuracy between them, although the false-positive-rate ratio differs.

fits_no_version.finding: Black-to-white false-positive-rate ratio rises with size from about 12B, reaching 1.5 (race excluded) and 2.21 (race included) at 52B, vs 1.92 for COMPAS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some fairness disparities in LM predictions grow with model size and depend on the prompt.

fits_no_version.finding: Detector-measured toxicity of generated text increases smoothly and significantly with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generated-text toxicity can increase with LM size.

fits_no_version.finding: Black-to-white predictive accuracy ratio shows no clear trend with size (Fig. 9); the largest models are slightly less fair than COMPAS (0.97).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some fairness metrics do not scale predictably with model size.

record.peer_reviewed: 2022 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT ’22)
record.problems: The paper states that the recommendation experiment is small and that the recidivism analysis has important dataset and fairness-metric caveats. Many plotted scaling values are not reported numerically in the text. The toxicity measure uses an automated detector, whose limitations the authors note.

untested.parts: No own pretraining-loss sweep; Fig. 1 is adapted from Kaplan et al.
No loss extrapolation from small runs is tested.
Other modalities and transfer are cited only.
No link of task performance to pretraining loss; no fitted functional form or quantified predictability; only two tasks; exact model sizes in the curves not stated.

missing.what: Black-to-white predictive accuracy ratio across model sizes: no clear trend, largest models slightly below COMPAS 0.97. Not a V6 measure, but an own result no row records.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'abrupt specific capability scaling' argument would limit V6, but it rests only on cited results (GPT-3 arithmetic, Gopher MMLU, program synthesis), so no verdict is drawn from it. Jared Kaplan, an author of an original source, is a co-author, but this paper is not itself an original source. Model sizes in Figs. 3, 5 and 8 are not listed; only 52B is named as the largest.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining-loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of whether small-run loss fits predict the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or fitted parameter/token exponents.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes are mentioned through prior work, not tested with the paper's own results.
The paper tests scaling with model size on recommendation and recidivism tasks; it does not test correlation with pretraining loss or broad downstream-task coverage.
No analysis of how fitting choices alter exponents or compute-optimal allocations.
